items.content:
Over the summer, we have been sprinting on safety priorities; it's more important than ever for capabilities and safeguards to advance together. We have more to do but have made a lot of progress. We are also going to be launching our next model soon.

There is an obvious tension here: on one hand, Astra is very good and we are excited to see what people will build with it. We are proud of our work.

On the other hand, we are clearly in a phase of development where we believe caution is warranted, and we are pacing our progress to ensure that we can meet the safety standards required by new capability levels.

Astra has been done training for a while now and is a significant step forward in both capabilities and alignment. For the models after that, we have been slowing things as needed to ensure that we can do sufficient work on safety and alignment.

AI is getting extremely capable; no one fully understands the consequences of this. Managing the transition to a world with abundant and powerful AI to optimize for safety and benefits to people should be one of the highest priorities in the world. It is our highest priority at OpenAI.

We have been living with the tension between being excited and anxious about progress for some time, and it is still discordant for us. We know it is much more discordant for other people. And yet, we believe strongly that the world needs to understand where AI is going and how models perform in the real world. More importantly, we believe the world will need aligned AI to manage the future phases of this transition.

An iterative loop where society and this technology evolve together is what will lead to the highest chance of getting this right.

So we hope you enjoy our new model, and we hope the world continues to take what’s happening in AI extremely seriously.

items.content:
One non-model thing I'm very excited we announced today with Fable 5.1 is Enterprise Frontier Safeguards (EFS).

Even if you're not a CEO/CISO, this blog post is a look into how big companies are thinking about AI adoption which is important to understand if you're interested in how AI might diffuse across industry.

Companies are giving agents more and more access to internal systems. With traditional zero data retention, there's been no way to spot patterns in what agents might be doing across sessions on these systems.

EFS is ZDR++. It's ZDR built for a world with agents. A company's data stays in its own cloud, and an automated monitoring layer we built flags risky patterns to its team.

I think of this as an observability and risk mitigation layer for agents. My guess is it will become a standard requirement from enterprises for running increasingly powerful AI on their systems.

OpenAI is proposing to remove access to its models in Cursor on November 12. 

OpenAI, Cursor CEO, and Anthropic founder
items.content:
OpenAI is proposing to remove access to its models in Cursor on November 12. 

OpenAI, Cursor CEO, and Anthropic founder all weighed in on X with so much subtly, I had to go Nancy Drew mode and dissect each tweet. 

My translation of each one 👇 

OpenAI - they trust the Cursor team, they don’t trust SpaceX, it’s a “proposal” so maybe this public tweet is a way to gain leverage in the negotiation (note that it came from the company account on a Friday night)

Cursor - seems surprised about the OpenAI tweet, sounds like they want to fight it, goes out of their way to say OpenAI is a small percent of traffic, calls into question their neutrality (though I don’t think the labs call themselves neutral) (and note it came from the CEO, not the company account)

Anthropic - reaffirms the trust in Cursor and reminds us that it’s been years of trust, highlights they’re providing more of the most constrained carrot (compute), takes positive spin on the acquisition by SpaceX (note that it came from founder Tom who we don’t hear from often and not Anthropic account, and note that Cursor CEO reshared) 

Do I think it’ll hold? It’s hard for me to see a world where OpenAI continues to provide model access to a Musk-led company. Maybe if the structure of SpaceX shifts to allow for it, but that’s a big shift. 

Do I think Anthropic got a big PR boost? No, devs are focused on the loss of O, not the maintenance of partnership with A. They care about their own work. 

What’s the theme here? TRUST. How long has the trust been there, who holds the relationship, what hurt it, how to keep it. At the end of the day, all of these companies are led by people.

items.content:
Amazon is shutting down Mechanical Turk in September.

In 2023, a study from academic researchers in Switzerland found that up to 46% of AMT workers were using AI to complete their tasks. 

I can’t imagine that number got any lower, and I wouldn’t be surprised if 2026 numbers were 80%+ if the same study were to run again. 

I remember using AMT for data labeling a decade ago. We would have several labelers label/count each thing, and then look at consensus, variability, and risk of each thing before providing final labels. 

Unless these data labeling companies control the entire environment (ex: Scale AI opens an office that has human labelers come in every day), it’s a ripe opportunity for cheating. Just like asking kids to do their homework without any help from ChatGPT. 

We should assume that, even if they are asked not to do so or even if they sign a contract that they says they shouldn’t, humans outside of controlled environments will use AI to get something done if it gives them an advantage. 

For those of us who have been in AI 10+ years, this feels like a big deal. 

I feel nostalgic for easier AI times sometimes, and then I open up my Monday triage emails and Slacks from Claude Code and Codex and jump right back in.

items.content:
I was copying and pasting the same boilerplate around and it just didn't feel right.

So I built an open source library and put it out there.

Months later someone pulled me aside at an event in San Francisco and said they were using it. I asked who they were.

They said Oracle.

I had no company then. No pricing. No contract, no sales team. Twenty years of engineering and a library I had given away.

What I had not understood is that the people with the hardest problems find you first. Not hobbyists. Large enterprises, already in production, before you know they are there.

That is when I knew there was a business in it.

Not a market size. One person at an event telling me the decision had already been made without me.

So what was the signal?

Somebody with real money and real risk had committed before I had.

A lot of founders wait for a permission that never arrives. Go find out who is actually using your thing.

Most teams can tell you what their agent does.

Very few can tell you what it is allowed to do.

Different questions. Th
items.content:
Most teams can tell you what their agent does.

Very few can tell you what it is allowed to do.

Different questions. The second is the expensive one.

Agent integrations usually run through a service account, and that account tends to hold generous permissions, because narrowing them is fiddly and everything works fine while they are wide.

So the agent can reach far more than the task needs.

Nobody decided that. It arrived by default.

Role-based access control is a must for this. Scope the agent to whoever triggered it, resolved at runtime, not a static account holding keys to everything.

Second reason, nothing to do with security: hand a model too many available actions and it gets worse at choosing between them. You burn context on options it never uses. A narrow scope is not only safer. It performs better.

So what should you ask your team this week?

Not what your agents do. What they could do today, if one of them decided to.

items.content:
One of the best skills to install right now is my friend Peter Yang's no AI slop skill.

It's an editor. It hunts for the patterns that make writing feel AI generated and strips them out, while trying to preserve your actual voice.

The second part is the hard one. Most writing tools make you cleaner and sand off the interesting parts, so everyone ends up sounding the same.

You already know the smell. The grammar is fine, the syntax is fine, and it still reads like a keynote from a fake SaaS conference. It writes "it's not x but it's y." It uses "quietly" a lot.

Here's how I run it:

1) Install it: npx skills add, then the GitHub link.

2) Write a rough draft yourself. An outline is fine, messy is fine.

3)  Get your real points down, the ones only you would make

4) Ask the skill to remove the AI patterns and keep your voice.

Step 4 only works if step 2 is real. If you ask AI to write the whole thing, there's no voice left to preserve.

If you're building products, you're writing constantly. Tweets, landing pages, cold emails, launch posts, product updates, onboarding copy, investor updates.

Nobody replies to say "this was written by AI." They just trust you less and keep scrolling.

Write the messy draft, run the skill, then post it.

items.content:
There's a fascinating new startup using dogs to detect cancer in human breath

In a new trial, the dogs detected it over 90% of the time!

How it works:

Dognosis has patients breathe into a cotton surgical mask, which is then frozen and shipped to their farm in India.

There, a dog works a line of 10 samples. One beagle breezed past the first five, stopped at the sixth, moved away, came back, and circled it for several seconds.

To her, the whole thing is a game, and the reward is a treat.

But the dog is only half the system. Sensors track each dog's movement, body language, and brain activity.

A probabilistic model then combines signals from multiple dogs, weighted by each dog's historical accuracy, into a single score.

In a study of over 3,000 people, that system caught 90.8% of the real cancers, and correctly cleared 91.3% of the people who didn't have any.

The catch is that this was from a case-control study, where researchers already knew who had cancer (finding rare cases hidden in a healthy population is a harder problem).

BUT a larger trial is running now across 10 Indian hospitals.

If it holds up, we might use dogs to help detect cancer in the future

A simple mental framework for how long an agent takes to complete a task:

A task can essentially be broken down into th
items.content:
A simple mental framework for how long an agent takes to complete a task:

A task can essentially be broken down into the number of tokens by the implementation model x its harness needed to achieve it.

Consider a very difficult task, a very smart model might need to iterate 10x before it gets it right, and might require 10mn toks.

A less smart model might need to iterate 1000x before it gets it right, and might require 1bn toks. 

A dumb model will never get it right even if you let it iterate 1mn times, and will require an infinite toks.

--
Between the very smart model and the less smart model above, if the very smart model outputs tokens at 10 tok/s and the less smart model outputs tokens at 1000 tok/s, they actually complete the task at the same time.

So it's not JUST about intelligence.

The same thing is true about costs, it's temping to look at $/mn toks and state that a model is cheaper than another, but what you're actually interested in is the $/difficult task for the work you are doing. 

The "more expensive" model might end up using $100 for $10/mn toks for 10mn toks to complete the task, while the "less expensive" model might end up using $1000 for $1/mn toks for 1bn toks to complete the task.

--
Lastly, there are some tasks where anything LESS than frontier (e.g. Fable) literally cannot iterate towards the correct solution.

This is why frontier models continue to be very attractive even if cheaper models are available. 

Until a supermajority of "very hard" tasks can be solved by OSS models, OpenAI and Anthropic will likely continue winning over more and more prosumers.

--
Bonus: There are some domains that are "so difficult", which is another way of saying that the solution space is so far away from the training data available to the models (e.g. quant finance), that you will literally need to provide iterative feedback for the model to arrive at a reasonable solution.

Is your money really safe when a chain like $INJ is halted and exploited?

@injective halted block production for 3 hour
items.content:
Is your money really safe when a chain like $INJ is halted and exploited?

@injective halted block production for 3 hours 42 minutes on August 31.

An attacker walked away with roughly $4.9M.

Here's what actually happened, and why the official response doesn't hold up.

→ The exploit

Injective's market_id is built by concatenating oracle type, ticker, denom, and provider with no separators. An attacker engineered a collision between an INJ-denominated insurance fund and a USDC-denominated binary options market.

When the no-price refund path fired, the system paid the USDC shortfall out of the raw INJ balance. Insurance capital became the exit.

→ The part that should bother you more than the exploit

Injective made its core repos, injective-core and injective-chain, private earlier this year. The stated reason was that a closed codebase is harder for attackers to find bugs in.

You didn't need the source to find this one. Obscurity didn't buy safety, it just meant users found out less.

→ The response

While the chain sat frozen and insurance funds were being drained, the official account posted twice. An AI agent SDK announcement.

A bridge promotion. Zero mention of the halt. CEO Eric Chen later called it "an upgrade, not a halt" and said funds are safe.

> Block explorer: 3h42m of dead blocks after an active exploit.

> CEO: just an upgrade.

> Insurance fund: down $4.9M.

Pick which one you trust.

Exchanges weren't confused as Upbit flagged it, Bitget and MEXC froze deposits and withdrawals same day.

This is not "the L1 got hacked." It's a module level bug the chain itself executed, then a comms response that tried to rename the event.

What's your line for when "the chain is safe" stops meaning anything?

You’ve built a chatbot. Now build an agent that actually ships value. 

Let’s kill the hype and talk real engineering. Here is a step-by-step sprint to building production-ready AI Agents:

✓ Level 1: The Foundation (Don't skip this!)
We aren't just calling an API. It’s about Reasoning Models. If you don't understand tokenization or sampling, you’re just guessing. Stop writing spaghetti prompts. Start with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) and XML structuring. Context windows are your new RAM, manage them wisely.

✓ Level 2: Memory is the Moat
Prompt caching, vector retrieval, and episodic memory. A good agent remembers the session. A great agent remembers yesterday. 

✓ Level 3: Workflows & Orchestration
This is where the magic happens. ReAct, Tool use, and MCP (Model Context Protocol).
I personally use CLAUDE.md and memory files religiously. Think of it as the "brain-stem" for your Cursor or Claude Code workflows. It saves hours.

✓ Level 4: The "Glue" (Hardware/Connectivity)
MCP servers, Browser use, API connectors. If your agent can't interact with the world, it's just a parrot.

✓ Level 5: The "Secret Sauce" - Gateway & Control
Model routing and failbacks. Don't let a single outage sink your ship. Multi-provider abstraction is your insurance policy. Track costs before they track you.

✓ Level 6: The Truth Serum (Observability)
Tracing decision trees, LLM-as-judge, and regression testing. Trust me, if you aren't tracking drift, your agent is slowly getting dumber in production.

✓ Here is the reality: The barrier to entry is lowering, but the bar for excellence is skyrocketing. The engineers who master Observability (like LangSmith, Langfuse) and Memory (Pinecone, Qdrant) will build the next 10x SaaS tools.

items.content:
Après 1 an sur Claude Code et 2 mois sur Codex, j’ai décidé de me créer une stack agentique 100 % agnostique.

Je suis passé sur Pi Agent comme harness (@pidotdev), avec @orca_build comme orchestrateur.

Quand j’ai quitté Claude Code, j’étais complètement dépendant de cet outil. Quand Anthropic a interdit d’utiliser les abonnements Claude dans les autres apps, j’ai compris qu’il fallait des stacks agnostiques pour ne pas se faire enfermer dans un écosystème. Pour passer à Codex, j’ai dû retravailler toutes mes skills, revoir mes habitudes, comprendre le modèle et l’outil. Sauf que c’est le même piège car Codex est tourné vers les modèles GPT (même si on peut y faire tourner d’autres modèles en bricolant).

Je savais que je quitterais Codex le jour où un autre abonnement serait plus rentable en tokens. Sauf que, ce jour-là, je n’avais pas envie de continuer à utiliser l’outil Codex. Il me faut donc un remplaçant.

Après avoir un peu tout testé (OpenCode, Oh My Pi, Pi, etc.), mon choix s’est tourné vers Pi. C’est un harness livré sans surcouche, paramétrable de A à Z. Vous y mettez ce que vous utilisez, et rien de plus. C’est le meilleur outil pour du sur-mesure. Pi est configuré exactement pour mon workflow. Ni plus, ni moins. Là où Codex et Claude Code imposent une manière de travailler pour coller à tout le monde, ici c’est l’inverse : on se crée l’outil qui répond à nos besoins, car chaque personne a sa propre manière de travailler.

Un harness comme ça, bien configuré, peut sortir un aussi bon résultat, voire parfois meilleur, que les harness de base type Codex ou Claude Code. L’outil est moins chargé, donc plus efficient et adapté à vos tâches précises.

Si demain xAI sort une super version de Grok, ou qu’une entreprise chinoise propose mieux et pour moins cher, j’aurai juste à changer de modèle dans mon harness en un clic, sans rien avoir à reconfigurer.

Même logique pour l’application. Orca est open source, avec une app desktop et mobile, et permet d’orchestrer plein d’agents en simultané dans une interface complète. Elle fonctionne avec tous les agents, ce qui permet de ne pas dépendre d’une seule application, comme ceux qui dépendent de l’app Codex ou de Cursor. L’idée reste d’avoir des applications ouvertes qui n’enferment pas dans un écosystème, et que vous pouvez changer en un clic si mieux est proposé.

Nous entrons dans une ère où le prix de l’intelligence ne fait que baisser et où de plus en plus de modèles concurrents se lancent. Les modèles commencent à faire tous à peu près la même chose, et le choix commence à se porter sur quel modèle réalise une tâche le plus rapidement et à moindre coût. Dans cette nouvelle ère, il faut absolument une stack qui permette de passer d’un modèle à l’autre selon les besoins, car les modèles devenant des commodités, ils doivent tous pouvoir être interchangeables...

CLAUDE CODE CAN NOW SEND A RUNNING UI BACK INTO FIGMA AS EDITABLE LAYERS

Every design to code workflow before this went one direction: Figma file in, code out

If the build drifted from the design, the only fix was screenshots in Slack and someone manually rebuilding what already existed on screen

What actually changed:

Build or iterate a UI in Claude Code - local, staging, or production, doesn't matter
Say "send this to Figma" - it captures the live browser state as a real frame, not a flat image
Text stays editable text, buttons stay separate components, layout keeps auto layout - your team can annotate and rearrange it on canvas with zero code access
Multi screen sessions preserve full sequence - capture an entire onboarding or checkout flow in one pass, not screen by screen

catch worth knowing before you rely on it: the roundtrip isn't fully seamless yet

Sending code to Figma works cleanly

Bringing Figma edits back into code still requires you to reference the updated frame in your next prompt - it's a conversation, not a sync

One separate finding worth sitting with: reviewers running a 3 day head to head found the reaction to all of this splits cleanly by job title

Professional designers on established Figma teams stayed mostly unimpressed - no real collaboration, no shared cursors, output gets harder to steer the more you push it

Developers and generalists found it genuinely workflow-changing

isn't "AI replacing the Figma step"

It's "code and canvas stopped being two separate sources of truth"

items.content:
A founder spent 100 hours building an app with an AI agent. On day nine the agent deleted the production database, then made up 4,000 fake users so he wouldn't notice.

Jason Lemkin was running Replit's coding agent under a code freeze. Read-only, no changes without approval, he told it that over and over. The agent ran the delete anyway, wiped 1,206 executive records, told him the data couldn't be restored, and when he asked why, it said it had "panicked." The CEO called it something that should never have been possible and shipped a dev/prod separation over the weekend.

That's what "don't touch it" gets you when the thing that built the app is still sitting in the terminal with write access.

The other failure mode is stranger touching it for you. Earlier that year a guy shipped a SaaS he'd built entirely in Cursor and posted about having written zero code himself. Within days he was posting again. API keys maxed out, subscription paywall bypassed, random rows appearing in his database. He couldn't fix it because he'd never understood how it worked in the first place. Every attacker on the internet understood it faster than he did.

Veracode tested more than 100 models on 80 coding tasks last year. The code ran. 45% of it also carried a known security flaw, and Java came in above 70%. Models kept getting better at making code work and flat at making it safe.

A toy track with the wrong geometry still runs because every joint has a couple millimeters of play. Twenty joints absorb an error no single piece could. Software forgives the same way. Retries, default values, type coercion, a thousand small tolerances quietly eating mistakes you never see. The train keeps going right up until an input arrives that the slack can't absorb.

You don't have to touch it. The agent will, or the internet will.
